column1: D-02,Donut,What are the main problems associated with OCR-dependent Visual Document Understanding methods?,Basic factual / retrieval,"The paper identifies three major problems with OCR-dependent VDU: high computational cost for OCR, inflexibility across languages and document/domain changes, and propagation of OCR errors into downstream VDU processing. The paper also discusses poor OCR quality for complex scripts such as Korean and Chinese and the added size/maintenance cost of post-OCR correction.","Donut.pdf, pp. 2–3","The main problems associated with OCR-dependent Visual Document Understanding (VDU) methods, as discussed in the context, include:
1. Quality of OCR for languages with complex character sets like Korean or Chinese is relatively low [50].
2. To deal with this, a post-OCR correction module is usually adopted, but it increases the entire system size and maintenance cost, making it impractical for real application environments.

3. The proposed method aims to address these problems by modeling a direct mapping from a raw input image to the desired output without OCR [8,9,29]. This new OCR-free VDU model is based on Transformer-only architecture, referred to as Document understanding transformer (Donut).

column1: D-06,Donut,How does information flow through Donut from the input document image to the final structured output?,Architecture / reasoning,"The input document image is processed by the visual encoder (Swin Transformer), which produces visual embeddings. 2. The encoded embeddings are then fed into the textual decoder module. This module maps the derived features into a sequence of subword tokens to construct a desired structured format (e.g., JSON). Each component of Donut is Transformer-based, and thus the model is trained easily in an end-to-end manner.
3. The final structured output provides the requested information in a specific format, such as the price of choco mochi being represented as ""14,000"" in JSON format.

In this context, there is no explicit evidence about how the decoder processes the image embeddings to generate the final structured output. However, it can be inferred that the decoder uses the information from the encoded embeddings to generate the desired structured format.

column1: D-11,Donut,"Using Figure 3, explain how Donut converts a document image into a structured JSON-like output.",Figure / visual understanding,"Figure 3 shows the image first entering Donut's Transformer visual encoder, which converts it into embeddings. The textual decoder uses those embeddings to generate a sequence of tokens. That output sequence is then converted into the target structured representation, such as JSON; the figure illustrates this with a receipt/question example.","Donut.pdf, pp. 4–5, Figure 3","Donut converts a document image into a structured JSON-like output by following the pipeline illustrated in Figure 3. The process involves two main components: a visual encoder and a textual decoder.

1. Visual Encoder: This component takes the input document image and converts it into a set of embeddings, denoted as {z}. In this study, Swin Transformer is used for the encoder network due to its superior performance in document parsing. The encoder splits the input image into non-overlapping patches, applies Swin Transformer blocks (consisting of a shifted window-based multi-head self-attention module and a two-layer MLP), and patch merging layers at each stage.

2. Textual Decoder: Given the embeddings {z}, the textual decoder generates a sequence of tokens (yi)*1, where y;€R” is an one-hot vector for the i-th token, v is the size of token vocabulary, and m is a hyperparameter, respectively. BART [33] is used as the decoder architecture. The decoder model weights are initialized with those from a publicly available pre-trained multi-lingual BART model.

The output token sequence is then converted to a desired structured format, specifically JSON, due to its high representation capacity. This conversion can be easily implemented using simple regular expressions. If the output token sequence is wrongly structured, fields are simply treated as lost. For example, if there is only [START name] exists but no [END name], it is assumed that the model fails to extract the ""name"" field.

column1: L1,LayoutLMv3,"What is the main purpose of LayoutLMv3, and what problem in Document AI pre-training does it aim to address?",Core understanding,"LayoutLMv3 aims to pre-train a multimodal Transformer for Document AI while addressing the mismatch between how text and image modalities are pre-trained in existing multimodal models. It uses unified discrete-token reconstruction objectives, MLM and MIM, together with WPA for cross-modal alignment, making the model applicable to both text-centric and image-centric Document AI tasks.","LayoutLMv3.pdf, pp. 1–2","The main purpose of LayoutLMv3 is to perform document analysis. Specifically, it aims to address the problem in Document AI pre-training related to multimodal representation learning by not relying on a pre-trained CNN or Faster R-CNN backbone for visual feature extraction and by using unified discrete token reconstructive objectives MLM and MIM to mitigate discrepancies between text and image representations. Additionally, it incorporates language modality in pre-training, which is effective in identifying smaller categories such as titles. (Reference: Pages 2, 4, 6, and 7 of LayoutLMv3.pdf)

1. Masked Language Modeling (MLM) learns language representation in a self-supervised manner, inspired by the masked language modeling in BERT [9] and masked visual-language modeling in LayoutLM.
2. Masked Image Modeling (MIM) is not explicitly mentioned in the provided context, so it's not specified what this objective learns.

3. Whole Pretext Approach (WPA) learns multimodal representation by combining text and image information in a self-supervised learning manner. The exact details of how WPA works are not specified in the provided context.

column1: VIT-02,Vision Transformer,How are the image patches converted into the input embeddings used by the Transformer encoder in ViT?,Architecture / Core Method,"Each fixed-size image patch is flattened and mapped to the Transformer’s constant D-dimensional latent space using a trainable linear projection. These patch embeddings are then combined with positional embeddings, with the learnable class token prepended.","Vision Transformer.pdf, p. 3","The image patches in Vision Transformer (ViT) are converted into input embeddings for the Transformer encoder as follows:
1. The original image is split into fixed-size patches.
2. Each patch is linearly embedded using a trainable linear projection. This results in a sequence of flattened 2D patch embeddings.
3. A learnable embedding, similar to BERT's [class] token, is prepended to the sequence of embedded patches.
4. Position embeddings are added to the patch embeddings to retain positional information. These position embeddings are standard learnable 1D embeddings.
5. The resulting sequence of embedding vectors serves as input to the Transformer encoder.

column1: VIT-06,Vision Transformer,What image-specific inductive biases does the standard Vision Transformer architecture introduce compared with convolutional neural networks?,Architecture vs CNN,"ViT deliberately introduces very few image-specific inductive biases compared with CNNs. Apart from the initial patch extraction, it does not impose CNN-style locality or translation equivariance; these patterns must largely be learned from data. This lack of inductive bias is a major reason ViT needs more data.","Vision Transformer.pdf, pp. 1–2","The standard Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture introduces several image-specific inductive biases compared to convolutional neural networks (CNNs). These differences are primarily due to its use of a Transformer encoder instead of the traditional convolutional layers.

1. Patch Embedding: Instead of using convolutions, ViT linearly embeds each patch of an image into a sequence of vectors. This allows the model to capture global dependencies between patches more effectively than CNNs, which primarily focus on local relationships.

2. Position Embeddings: To retain positional information in the transformed sequence, ViT adds learnable 1D position embeddings to the patch embeddings. This is different from CNNs, where positional information is implicitly encoded through convolutional filters and pooling operations.

3. Self-Attention Mechanism: The Transformer encoder uses a multi-head self-attention (MSA) mechanism, which allows the model to focus on multiple relevant patches simultaneously. In contrast, CNNs rely on weight sharing and local receptive fields to capture relationships between patches.

4. Global Dependencies: Due to its ability to handle global dependencies more effectively, ViT can potentially learn more abstract representations of images compared to CNNs, which primarily focus on local features.

5. Scalability: The Transformer architecture is designed to be scalable and efficient, allowing for the use of large models with billions of parameters. This is in contrast to CNNs, where increasing model size can lead to computational challenges due to the need for larger kernels and more complex architectures.
It's important to note that these differences may result in both advantages and disadvantages compared to CNNs, depending on the specific task and dataset at hand.

column1: CLIP-04,CLIP,How does CLIP learn to associate images with their corresponding textual descriptions during pre-training?,Contrastive Learning,"CLIP jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder with a contrastive objective. The model is trained on large-scale datasets containing both images and their corresponding captions, allowing it to learn a shared embedding space where images and texts can be compared effectively.

column1: CLIP-05,CLIP,What are the roles of the image encoder and text encoder in CLIP?,Contrastive Learning,"The image encoder converts an input image into a feature representation, while the text encoder converts the corresponding text into a feature representation. Both are projected into the same multimodal embedding space so their representations can be compared.","CLIP.pdf, pp. 4–5","The image encoder and text encoder play crucial roles in the Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) model.

1. Image Encoder: It takes an input of aligned images, processes them to extract feature representations of each modality. This is done by passing the images through a learned projection (W_i) and then applying normalization and dot product operations. The image encoder used in CLIP is either a ResNet or a Vision Transformer (ViT).

2. Text Encoder: It takes an input of aligned texts, which are typically lower-cased byte pair encoded representations. The text encoder operates on this text representation and extracts feature representations similar to the image encoder. The text encoder used in CLIP is a Transformer with modifications described by Radford et al. (2019). It operates on a 49,152 vocab size and has a base size of a 63M-parameter 12-layer 512-wide model with 8 attention heads.

Both encoders then project the feature representations into a joint multimodal embedding space, where they can be compared to determine if the image and text are semantically related or not. This comparison is done using scaled pairwise cosine similarities, and the model is trained using a symmetric loss function.

column1: CLIP-06,CLIP,How are image and text representations compared during CLIP's training and zero-shot prediction?,Contrastive Learning,"CLIP compares L2-normalized image and text embeddings using cosine similarity. column1: CLIP-07,CLIP,How does CLIP perform zero-shot image classification without being explicitly trained on the target classification dataset?,Zero-Shot Classification,"CLIP performs zero-shot classification by converting the target dataset's class concepts into natural-language text descriptions. It embeds the image and candidate class texts with the two encoders, compares their similarities, and selects the most probable class without training on the target dataset's labeled examples.","CLIP.pdf, pp. 6–7","CLIP performs zero-shot image classification by learning a mapping between text and images during pre-training. It achieves this without being explicitly trained on the target classification dataset by using a large-scale dataset of paired text and image data, such as YFCC100M or WIT. The model is then evaluated on various datasets for zero-shot performance, which shows how well it can classify images from these datasets based solely on the learned text embeddings.

The paper mentions that CLIP's zero-shot performance varies across different datasets, with some datasets like Flowers and Birdsnap performing better than others like GTSRB and Stanford Cars. The authors attribute these differences to the relative density of relevant data in each pre-training dataset. They also note that their approach can potentially use any reasonably filtered collection of paired (text, image) data, as demonstrated by their custom dataset.

However, they also mention issues with duplicate detection using the model's learned embedding space, which led them to develop a new near-duplicate detector. This detector uses a synthetic data augmentation pipeline that combines various common image manipulations and trains a ResNet-50 model to maximize similarity between an image and its transformed variant while minimizing similarity to all other images in a training batch. The modified model achieves nearly 100% accuracy on its proxy training task.

column1: RAG-01,RAG,"What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and what problem is it designed to address?",Core / Architecture,"RAG is a retrieval-augmented generation framework that combines a pre-trained parametric seq2seq generator with a non-parametric external memory accessed by a neural retriever. It is designed for knowledge-intensive language tasks, addressing limitations of purely parametric language models such as difficulty updating/revising knowledge and increased risk of unsupported or hallucinated information.","RAG.pdf, pp. 1–2","Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a method that augments the input space of Language Models (LMs) with retrieved text passages. It is designed to improve performance on knowledge-intensive tasks after fine-tuning or used with off-the-shelf LMs (Guu et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Ram et al., 2023). The specific problem it addresses is the need for LMs to have access to a larger and more diverse range of information during language generation.

column1: BERT-01,BERT,"What does BERT stand for, and what is the main idea behind the model?",Core / Architecture,"BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. It is a deep bidirectional Transformer representation model pre-trained on unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on left and right context in all layers, then fine-tuned with minimal task-specific architecture for downstream NLP tasks.","BERT.pdf, pp. 1–8, 13–16","BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. The main idea behind the model is to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. This allows the pre-trained BERT model to be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications.",YES,CORRECT,,,Supported=2

BERT-04,BERT,Why does the masked language model allow BERT to learn bidirectional representations while a traditional left-to-right language model cannot?,Core / Architecture,MLM enables bidirectional pre-training because the model predicts selected masked tokens while conditioning on both left and right context. A conventional left-to-right language model cannot use both directions simultaneously because bidirectional conditioning would allow the target word to see itself and make prediction trivial.,"BERT.pdf, pp. 1–8, 13–16","The masked language model allows BERT to learn bidirectional representations because it enables pre-training of deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. The masked language model randomly masks some of the tokens from the input, and the objective is to predict the original vocabulary id of the masked tokens, which allows BERT to learn bidirectional representations. BERT-07,BERT,"How do BERT, OpenAI GPT, and ELMo differ in their approaches to obtaining contextual representations?",Training / Comparison,"BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer jointly conditioned on left and right context in all layers; GPT uses a left-to-right Transformer; ELMo concatenates independently trained left-to-right and right-to-left LSTM representations. BERT and GPT are fine-tuning approaches, while ELMo is feature-based.","BERT.pdf, pp. 1–8, 13–16","BERT, OpenAI GPT, and ELMo differ in their approaches to obtaining contextual representations as follows:

1. BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer, which means it considers both left and right context in all layers. In contrast, OpenAI GPT uses a left-to-right Transformer, where every token can only attend to context to its left. ELMo, on the other hand, uses the concatenation of independently trained left-to-right and right-to-left LSTMs to generate features for downstream tasks.

2. BERT and OpenAI GPT are fine-tuning approaches, while ELMo is a feature-based approach. This means that BERT and OpenAI GPT learn to predict missing words in a sentence based on both left and right context during the pre-training phase, and then these models can be further trained (or fine-tuned) for specific tasks like classification, question answering, etc. ELMo, however, generates fixed-length feature vectors for each word that are learned from unlabeled text during the pre-training phase, and these features can be used as input to various downstream tasks without further training.",YES,PARTIAL,Generation,,Supported=1
